---
title: "Rust Types"
---


Rust's type system will feel partly like C# (static, value vs. reference semantics) and partly like Dart 3 (sealed classes and pattern matching), but it adds one new idea: **every value has exactly one owner, and the type tells you where the data lives**. Keep that in mind as we go.

## 1. The big picture

```
                         Rust Types
                             │
      ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┐
      │                      │                          │
   Scalar               Compound                  Custom (yours)
 (single value)    (fixed group, built-in)              │
      │                      │                   ┌──────┴──────┐
  i32, u8, f64,        tuple  (i32, f64)       struct         enum
  bool, char           array  [i32; 5]       (AND: has      (OR: is one
                                              all fields)    of variants)
      │
      └─────────── all live on the STACK (fixed size, known at compile time)

                    Standard Library Collections (growable, HEAP)
       String, Vec<T>, HashMap<K,V>, HashSet<T>, VecDeque<T>, BTreeMap<K,V> ...
```

## 2. Scalar types

```rust
let a: i32 = -42;        // signed integer (default for integers)
let b: u8 = 255;         // unsigned, 0..=255
let c: usize = 10;       // pointer-sized unsigned; used for indexing/lengths
let d: f64 = 3.14;       // 64-bit float (default for floats)
let e: bool = true;
let f: char = '狗';      // 4 bytes, any Unicode scalar value (Thai works too: 'ก')
```

| Size | Signed | Unsigned |
|---|---|---|
| 8-bit | `i8` | `u8` |
| 16-bit | `i16` | `u16` |
| 32-bit | `i32` | `u32` |
| 64-bit | `i64` | `u64` |
| 128-bit | `i128` | `u128` |
| pointer-sized | `isize` | `usize` |

There are two things that will surprise you coming from Python and R.

**No implicit conversion.** Even `i32 + i64` is a compile error, so you convert explicitly:

```rust
let x: i32 = 5;
let y: i64 = 10;
let z = x as i64 + y;          // `as` is a raw cast (can truncate!)
let w: u8 = 300_i32.try_into().unwrap_or(255); // safe, checked conversion
```

**Overflow is a bug, not a silent wrap.** In debug builds, `255u8 + 1` panics. In release builds it wraps. If you want specific behavior, you say so:

```rust
let n: u8 = 250;
n.checked_add(10);     // None        (returns Option<u8>)
n.wrapping_add(10);    // 4           (modular arithmetic)
n.saturating_add(10);  // 255         (clamps at max)
```

## 3. Compound types: tuple and array

```rust
// Tuple: fixed length, mixed types
let point: (i32, f64, char) = (1, 2.5, 'x');
let (a, b, c) = point;        // destructuring
println!("{}", point.1);      // 2.5

// Array: fixed length, single type, length is PART of the type
let arr: [i32; 5] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let zeros = [0u8; 100];       // 100 zeros
println!("{}", arr[0]);       // bounds-checked at runtime → panics if out of range

// Unit type: an empty tuple, like `void` in C#
let nothing: () = ();
```

`[i32; 5]` and `[i32; 6]` are **different types**. If you need a growable list, use `Vec<T>` (section 6).

## 4. Stack vs. heap

Rust makes memory layout part of the type, so the following model is worth getting into your head early:

```
let n: i32 = 7;
let v: Vec<i32> = vec![10, 20, 30];
let s: String = String::from("hello");

        STACK                              HEAP
  ┌──────────────────┐
n │ 7                │
  ├──────────────────┤
v │ ptr ─────────────┼──────────►  [10][20][30][  ]   (capacity 4)
  │ len = 3          │
  │ cap = 4          │
  ├──────────────────┤
s │ ptr ─────────────┼──────────►  [h][e][l][l][o]    (UTF-8 bytes)
  │ len = 5          │
  │ cap = 5          │
  └──────────────────┘
   fixed size,                      growable,
   known at compile time            size known at runtime
```

`Vec<T>` and `String` are both small 24-byte "handles" on the stack that own a heap buffer. When the owner goes out of scope, the heap buffer is freed automatically. There's no garbage collector like in C#, Python, or R, and you never call `free` manually as in C.

## 5. Strings: `String` vs `&str`

This is the #1 confusion for newcomers.

```
String   = owned, growable, heap buffer      (like StringBuilder that you own)
&str     = borrowed "view" into UTF-8 bytes  (ptr + len, read-only)

let owned: String = String::from("hello world");
let view: &str = &owned[0..5];       // "hello"
let literal: &str = "baked into binary";

  owned ──► [h][e][l][l][o][ ][w][o][r][l][d]
             ▲
  view  ─────┘  len = 5      (no copy, just a window)
```

```rust
fn greet(name: &str) {            // accept &str: works with both kinds
    println!("Hello, {name}");
}

let s = String::from("KS");
greet(&s);          // &String auto-converts to &str
greet("LB");        // literal is already &str
```

A good rule of thumb is to **take `&str` as a parameter and return `String`** when you're creating new text.

There's also a quirk here: `s[0]` doesn't compile, because UTF-8 characters are 1–4 bytes, so "the 0th character" isn't an O(1) operation. Use `s.chars().nth(0)` or iterate with `.chars()` instead.

## 6. Slices: the general pattern behind `&str`

A slice `&[T]` is a borrowed view into contiguous data, whether that's an array, a `Vec`, or part of either:

```rust
let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let middle: &[i32] = &v[1..4];   // [2, 3, 4]

fn sum(xs: &[i32]) -> i32 {      // accepts arrays AND Vecs
    xs.iter().sum()
}
sum(&v);
sum(&[10, 20]);
```

```
  Owned          Borrowed view
  ─────          ─────────────
  String    →    &str
  Vec<T>    →    &[T]
  [T; N]    →    &[T]
```

## 7. Custom types: `struct` and `enum`

### Struct ("has all of these fields")

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]   // auto-implement printing, cloning, ==
struct Patient {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    age: u8,
}

impl Patient {
    // associated function (like a static constructor in C#)
    fn new(id: u32, name: &str, age: u8) -> Self {
        Self { id, name: name.to_string(), age }
    }

    // method: &self = read-only borrow of the instance
    fn is_adult(&self) -> bool {
        self.age >= 18
    }
}

// Tuple struct and unit struct
struct Meters(f64);     // "newtype" pattern: type-safe wrapper
struct Marker;          // no data

let p = Patient::new(1, "Somchai", 45);
println!("{:?} adult={}", p, p.is_adult());
```

Data (`struct`) and behavior (`impl`) are separate blocks, and there's **no inheritance**. Shared behavior comes from **traits**, which are like C# interfaces.

### Enum ("is exactly one of these variants")

This is Rust's superpower. It's closest to **Dart 3 sealed classes**, since each variant can carry different data:

```rust
enum Shape {
    Circle { radius: f64 },
    Rectangle { w: f64, h: f64 },
    Triangle(f64, f64, f64),
}

impl Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        match self {                       // must handle EVERY variant
            Shape::Circle { radius } => std::f64::consts::PI * radius * radius,
            Shape::Rectangle { w, h } => w * h,
            Shape::Triangle(a, b, c) => {
                let s = (a + b + c) / 2.0;
                (s * (s - a) * (s - b) * (s - c)).sqrt()
            }
        }
    }
}
```

If you later add `Shape::Hexagon`, every `match` that doesn't handle it becomes a **compile error**. That's what makes refactoring safe.

### The two most important enums: `Option` and `Result`

Rust has **no null** and **no exceptions**. Instead:

```rust
enum Option<T> { Some(T), None }          // value may be absent
enum Result<T, E> { Ok(T), Err(E) }       // operation may fail
```

```rust
fn find_age(name: &str) -> Option<u8> {
    if name == "KS" { Some(40) } else { None }
}

fn parse_age(text: &str) -> Result<u8, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    text.parse::<u8>()
}

match find_age("KS") {
    Some(age) => println!("Age: {age}"),
    None => println!("Not found"),
}

// The ? operator: "return the error early, otherwise unwrap"
fn double_age(text: &str) -> Result<u16, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    let age = parse_age(text)?;       // like try/catch, but explicit in the type
    Ok(age as u16 * 2)
}
```

```
  C# / Python / R             Rust
  ──────────────              ────
  null / None / NULL    →     Option<T>   (compiler forces you to check)
  throw / raise / stop  →     Result<T,E> (error is part of the signature)
```

## 8. Standard collections

```rust
use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet, VecDeque, BTreeMap};

// Vec<T>: growable array, used 90% of the time
let mut v: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
v.push(1);
v.extend([2, 3]);
let doubled: Vec<i32> = v.iter().map(|x| x * 2).collect();

// HashMap<K, V>
let mut scores: HashMap<String, u32> = HashMap::new();
scores.insert("Alice".to_string(), 90);
*scores.entry("Bob".to_string()).or_insert(0) += 5;   // upsert idiom
if let Some(s) = scores.get("Alice") { println!("{s}"); }

// HashSet<T>
let tags: HashSet<&str> = ["ct", "mri", "ct"].into_iter().collect(); // {"ct","mri"}

// VecDeque<T>: fast push/pop at both ends (queue)
let mut q: VecDeque<i32> = VecDeque::new();
q.push_back(1);
q.push_front(0);
q.pop_front();

// BTreeMap<K, V>: sorted by key
let mut sorted: BTreeMap<u32, &str> = BTreeMap::new();
sorted.insert(3, "c");
sorted.insert(1, "a");   // iterates in order: 1, 3
```

| Rust | Python | C# | R |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Vec<T>` | `list` | `List<T>` | atomic vector / `list` |
| `[T; N]` | (none) | `T[]` (fixed) | — |
| `HashMap<K,V>` | `dict` | `Dictionary<K,V>` | named list / env |
| `BTreeMap<K,V>` | (sorted dict, 3rd-party) | `SortedDictionary<K,V>` | — |
| `HashSet<T>` | `set` | `HashSet<T>` | `unique()` |
| `VecDeque<T>` | `collections.deque` | `Queue<T>` / `LinkedList<T>` | — |
| `BinaryHeap<T>` | `heapq` | `PriorityQueue<T,P>` | — |
| `struct` | `@dataclass` | `struct` / `record` | `list` / S4 |
| `enum` with data | (no direct equivalent) | class hierarchy | — |

## 9. A quick mental summary

```
 Need one value?                → scalar (i32, f64, bool, char)
 Fixed small group, mixed?      → tuple
 Fixed count, same type?        → array [T; N]
 Growable list?                 → Vec<T>
 Text you own / text you read?  → String / &str
 Read-only view of a sequence?  → &[T]
 Named fields?                  → struct
 "One of several shapes"?       → enum + match
 Maybe missing? Might fail?     → Option<T> / Result<T, E>
 Key → value lookup?            → HashMap (fast) / BTreeMap (sorted)
```

You can run all of these snippets instantly at **play.rust-lang.org** without installing anything. Locally, `cargo new playground && cargo run` gets you started.

The `&`, `mut`, and "owns the heap buffer" ideas above all come from **ownership and borrowing**, which is the natural next topic and the key to why `String` vs `&str` exists.
